name: Horsetail extract
lead: Horsetail extract is prepared from Equisetum arvense (field or common horsetail), a perennial non-flowering plant native to northern temperate regions [1]. It is marketed in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a source of silica, with the plant reported to contain silicon along with flavonoids, saponins, tannins and minerals [1].

Wikipedia describes evidence for its medicinal properties as limited, with laboratory data suggesting anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial activity [1]. No published human trial reviewed here has shown an effect of horsetail alone on hair growth, though at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements [3][4].

paras: Austrian herbal tradition used horsetail tea, baths and compresses for skin, kidney and joint complaints, Finnish folk medicine valued its silicic acid, and it was historically used to strengthen fingernails [1]. The plant has also been used to polish pewter and wood because of its abrasive stems [1].

A laboratory study of a standardized commercial E. arvense extract reported effects on human lymphocyte function in vitro, consistent with the plant's European use for inflammatory disorders [2]. A rat study reported SIRT1-related effects on insulin sensitivity in induced diabetes [5]. A 2025 qualitative review of alopecia misinformation is among the literature that discusses unproven hair remedies [6].
Wikipedia notes that horsetail is toxic to livestock, particularly horses, and that the plant may synthesize nicotine under polluted conditions [1].
No studies found of horsetail extract on its own for hair loss or hair growth in humans.

Two registered trials, NCT06841458 (n=45, androgenetic alopecia, recruiting) and NCT06174441 (n=89, hair thinning, completed 2024), test dietary supplements for hair; the listings reviewed here do not establish horsetail as a sole active ingredient, and no results are summarized [3][4].

lore.intro: Horsetail is mentioned in hair-supplement marketing and natural-hair discussions mainly as a silica source.

claims.claim: Horsetail silica strengthens hair and supports growth
claims.believers: Proponents of herbal hair care say the plant's silicon content supports hair and nails, echoing its folk use for nail strength [1].
claims.experts: Reviews describe evidence for medicinal effects of horsetail as limited, and no published trial has tested horsetail alone for hair [1].

card.summary: A silica-rich herbal extract sold for hair and nails, with limited lab data and no single-ingredient hair trials.
card.note: Plant is toxic to livestock; human hair evidence is lacking.

quick.overview:
Horsetail extract comes from a fern-like plant and is promoted in hair supplements and shampoos for its silica content. Its folk use includes strengthening nails.

No human trial of horsetail alone has shown a hair benefit, so its appearance effect is unproven.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in cells. A silica-to-hair pathway is the usual proposal but has not been tested in published human trials.
quick.risks: The plant is toxic to livestock and may form nicotine in polluted conditions. Human safety data for hair-focused use are limited.
